lessons.title: Count what can happen

steps.headline: To find a probability, list every equally likely outcome and count the ones you want.

lead.text: Two flips can land four ways: HH, HT, TH, TT. Each way is an outcome. A group of outcomes you care about is an event, such as “exactly one head”.
That event holds HT and TH: 2 outcomes out of 4. Counting like this only works when every outcome is equally likely.
Roll two dice, one after the other. The grid shows the first roll down the side and the second across the top. Each cell is one ordered outcome.

reveal.text: Whatever you predicted, the grid has 6 rows of 6 cells. (1,6) and (6,1) are different cells.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice total 7.

workedSteps.text: List the pairs that make 7.
Count them. That is the top of the fraction.
Divide by every ordered pair.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice total 8.

workedSteps.text: A first roll of 2 needs a second roll of 6. Go along the first rolls.
Count the pairs.
Divide by all 36 pairs.

lead.text: An event can hold several totals. “At least 10” means a total of 10, 11 or 12. Count each matching pair once, and divide by the same 36.

reveal.text: You counted matching cells, then divided by the whole grid. Several totals can sit inside one event.

lead.text: Every pair either makes at least 10 or does not. No pair is in both groups. The two groups together fill the grid.

reveal.text: You did not recount the grid. What an event leaves out is its complement, and the two probabilities fill the whole.

lessons.orientation: Use equally likely ordered outcomes to calculate a probability, and avoid treating possible sums as equally likely.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: You flip a coin twice and write down what you see, like HT for heads then tails.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a probability by counting equally likely outcomes, and know why totals are not equally likely.

recap.keyIdea: When outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number of all outcomes.

blocks.text: You listed 36 ordered outcomes for two dice and found that 6 of them make a total of 7. Then you found 6 of 36 reach at least 10, and 30 do not.

recap.nextHook: Someone tells you the first die showed 1 or 2. What happens to the 36?

lessons.title: When the condition changes

steps.headline: A clue shortens the list of possible outcomes. Count inside the shorter list.

lead.text: “At least one head” crosses out TT. The results left are the only ones that could have happened. A probability found inside that shorter list is a conditional probability. Words like “given” or “knowing that” signal one.
The new list sets the denominator. The favourable outcomes are counted inside it.
Back to the grid of two dice. You learn the first die showed 1 or 2. The faded rows are no longer possible.

reveal.text: Two rows of six cells remain. The clue changed the number of possible outcomes from 36 to the count you found.

steps.headline: Given a first roll of at most 2, find the probability of a second roll of at most 4.

workedSteps.text: Keep only the two surviving rows. Count their pairs.
Count the pairs in those rows with a second roll of at most 4.
Divide favourable by possible.

steps.headline: Given a first roll of at most 2, find the probability of a second roll of at most 3.

workedSteps.text: Two rows survive, so 12 pairs are possible.
Count the pairs with a second roll of at most 3.
Divide by the 12 possible pairs.

lead.text: Now ask about the total instead of one die. The pairs still come only from the surviving rows.

reveal.text: You looked only inside the surviving rows, and divided by their pairs. The clue decides where to count.

lead.text: A tighter clue leaves less. The first die is known to be 1, so one row survives.

reveal.text: A tighter clue leaves a shorter list. Restrict first, then count the event inside it.

lessons.orientation: Restrict the possible outcomes before computing a conditional probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: You flip two coins. A friend peeks and says at least one landed heads.

intro.promise: By the end you'll shrink the list of possible outcomes when you get a clue, and find a probability inside what is left.

recap.keyIdea: A clue shrinks the list of possible outcomes. A conditional probability counts the favourable outcomes inside the shorter list and divides by its size.

blocks.text: You cut 36 pairs down to 12 once you knew the first die was at most 2. Then you found that 3 of those 12 reach a total of 7 or more.

recap.nextHook: Does a clue always change the chances? Sometimes it tells you nothing.

lessons.title: Independent repetitions

steps.headline: For independent events, the chance that both happen is the two chances multiplied.

lead.text: A coin flip cannot change a die roll. Events like that are independent: learning one result leaves the other's chance as it was. Heads is 1/2 and a 3 is 1/6.
The chance of both is 1/2 × 1/6. You can check it on the grid of 12 results from the hook.
Roll two fair dice. The green square marks the pairs where both rolls are at most 3. Think about how big it looks next to the whole grid.

reveal.text: The square is 3 cells by 3, so 9 of 36. Each die is at most 3 with chance 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 agrees with your count.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice both show at most 4.

workedSteps.text: One die: four of the six values qualify.
The dice are independent, so multiply the chances.
Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice both show at most 2.

workedSteps.text: One die: find the chance of at most 2.
Multiply the two chances.

lead.text: The same rule works for different kinds of event. Find each chance on its own, then multiply them.

reveal.text: You used the same rule on a coin and a die. Find each chance alone, then multiply.

steps.headline: Events that cannot happen together are not independent.

lead.text: Roll one die. “It shows 1” and “it shows 2” cannot both happen. Events like that are mutually exclusive. If you learn the die showed 1, you know it did not show 2.
Back to two dice. “At least one is above 3” is easy to count the other way round: it is everything except “both at most 3”.

reveal.text: You did not list the pairs. You took the complement of the both-low event, which independence let you find.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events, and calculate a joint probability.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: You flip a coin and roll a die, and write down both results together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply the chances of independent events, and tell independent events from ones that cannot both happen.

recap.keyIdea: When events are independent, the chance that both happen is the product of their chances. Events that cannot happen together are not independent.

blocks.text: You found that both dice at most 3 has chance 9/36, the same as 1/2 × 1/2. Then you multiplied again to get 1/9 for both at most 2.

recap.nextHook: Now from chance to data. What is a typical value in a list of numbers?

lessons.title: Centre and outliers

steps.headline: The mean shares the total equally. The median is the middle of the sorted list.

lead.text: Sharing a total equally gives the mean: add everything, divide by how many. The median is the middle value once the list is in order. A value far from the rest is an outlier.
For 2, 4, 4, 5 and 5, both centres are 4.
The mean uses every value. The median uses only their order. Now the last 5 is swapped for a far larger value.

reveal.text: The total jumped by 20, so the mean went from 4 to 8. The middle value did not move. An outlier drags the mean and barely touches the median.

steps.headline: Find the median of 9, 2, 5, 3 and 7.

workedSteps.text: Put the values in order, smallest first.
There are five values, so the middle is the third.
The median is that value.

steps.headline: Find the median of 10, 2, 6 and 4.

workedSteps.text: Sort the values.
Four values have two in the middle: the second and third. Add them.
Halve that total to average the pair.

lead.text: Now the values are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25. Put them in order and take the middle one.

reveal.text: The 25 changed the mean a lot and the median not at all. The median only needs the order.

lead.text: An estate agent wants the typical price from five recent sales. One was a mansion. Give the median, so the mansion cannot skew it.

reveal.text: You can say what is typical without being fooled by one extreme sale. The mean would have been dragged upwards.

lessons.orientation: Calculate the mean and median, and see how one extreme observation changes them differently.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: Five friends put their money in a pot and share it out equally.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the mean and median of a list, and say which one a single extreme value moves.

recap.keyIdea: The mean is the total shared equally and uses every value. The median is the middle of the sorted list. An outlier drags the mean and barely moves the median.

blocks.text: You shared £20 among five friends and got a mean of 4. Swap one 5 for 25 and the mean becomes 8, while the median stays 4.

recap.nextHook: Two lists can have the same centre and still look nothing alike. What else describes them?

lessons.title: Same centre, different spread

steps.headline: The range is the largest value minus the smallest. It measures spread.

lead.text: The gap you just found has a name: the range. It is one way to measure spread, how far apart the values lie. Both buses have the same mean, yet their gaps differ.
The first list is 4, 4, 4, 4. The second is 2, 2, 6, 6. Work out each mean, then picture where the points sit.

reveal.text: Both have mean 4. The four 4s sit on one spot. The 2s and 6s lie two either side. Same centre, different spread.

steps.headline: The standard deviation is the typical distance from the mean.

lead.text: To use every value, measure each distance from the mean and square it. The average of those squares is the variance. Its square root is the standard deviation, in the data's own units.
Each list here is a whole population, so divide by the count. A sample usually divides by one less.

steps.headline: Find the population variance of 1, 1, 1 and 9.

workedSteps.text: Find the mean: the total over the count.
Square each distance from the mean.
These are 4, 4, 4 and 36. Add them and divide by four.

steps.headline: Find the population standard deviation of 2, 2, 6 and 6.

workedSteps.text: The mean is 4. Every value is 2 away, so every squared distance is 2 × 2.
Add the squared distances.
Divide by how many values there are.
Take the square root.

lead.text: Same steps, new numbers. The mean is still 4, but the values sit further out.

reveal.text: You found each distance, squared it and averaged. A wider list gives a larger variance with the same mean.

lead.text: Back to Bus B, late 0, 0, 20 and 20 minutes. Treat the four days as the whole population. Bus A, always 10 minutes late, has a standard deviation of zero.

reveal.text: The standard deviation is in minutes, the same units as the data. Two buses with the same mean are told apart.

lessons.orientation: Compare datasets with the same mean, and distinguish range from population variance and standard deviation.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: Two buses both average 10 minutes late. Look at how differently they get there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell two lists with the same mean apart, using the range and the standard deviation.

recap.keyIdea: The range uses only the largest and smallest values. The variance and standard deviation use every value's distance from the mean, so lists with the same mean can differ in spread.

blocks.text: You compared 4, 4, 4, 4 with 2, 2, 6, 6. Both have mean 4. For 2, 2, 6, 6 the range is 4 and the standard deviation is 2.

recap.nextHook: You rarely measure a whole population. What can a sample tell you about it?

lessons.title: Samples and populations

steps.headline: A population is everyone you want to learn about. A sample is the part you measure.

lead.text: In the shop survey, the 12 customers are the population. The morning shoppers you asked are a sample of it. We usually measure a sample because measuring everyone costs too much.
Here is a small population of shoppers. Only the checked members enter a sample. Think about who belongs to the population.

reveal.text: Whatever you counted, the unchecked members belong to the population too.

steps.headline: Five members are worth 2 and five are worth 6. Find the population mean.

workedSteps.text: Count every member of the population.
Add all the values.
Divide the total by the members.

steps.headline: Six members are worth 2 and six are worth 8. Find the population mean.

workedSteps.text: Count the members.
Add all the values.
Divide the total by 12.

lead.text: Now take a sample that has three members from each group. Work out its mean, then compare it with the population.

reveal.text: You compared a sample with its population. This balanced sample reaches the population's mean.

steps.headline: How you choose a sample matters more than how big it is.

lead.text: A sample chosen by chance, where every member has a known, non-zero chance of selection, is a probability sample. A method that leaves a group out is biased, and asking more of the same group does not fix it. One lucky match proves nothing.
The group values are now 4 and 10. A survey that reached only one group would miss the other. Find the population mean, the figure a good sample is trying to reach.

reveal.text: You found the target a sample is aiming for. Define who you want to learn about before deciding whom to measure.

lessons.orientation: Identify a population, compare selection methods and explain why a large biased sample can still mislead.
lessons.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: A shop owner wants to know what customers spend, so she surveys the morning shoppers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a population from a sample, and say why a large sample can still mislead.

recap.keyIdea: A sample is only the part you measure. If the method leaves part of the population out, a large sample still misleads.

blocks.text: You saw the morning shoppers alone give a mean of 2, while the whole population's mean was 5. A balanced sample of three from each group gave 5.

recap.nextHook: That completes the toolkit: counting chances, centres, spread and samples. Where will you use it first?

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice, one after the other. How many ordered outcomes are possible?
hints: Count the rows, then the cells in each row.
Each first-roll value can pair with every second-roll value.
Multiply the number of first-roll choices by the number of second-roll choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 first rolls and 6 second rolls, giving 6 × 6 = 36 ordered outcomes.

questions.onCorrect: 36. Each of the 6 first rolls pairs with all 6 second rolls, so you multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two dice. Each first roll pairs with every second roll, so the counts combine another way.
That is one die. The grid lists both rolls together, one cell per pair.

questions.prompt: Only (1,1) makes a total of 2. Why is a total of 7 more likely?
hints: Compare how many cells match each total.

acceptedIdeas: More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Six equally likely ordered pairs total 7, whereas only (1, 1) totals 2. Probabilities depend on the number of matching pairs, not just the list of possible sums.

choices.label: Every possible sum is equally likely
More ordered pairs make 7 than make 2
The second die always makes large totals

questions.onCorrect: Six pairs make 7 and one makes 2. Totals with more pairs are more likely.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the cells for each total. If every sum were equally likely, the cell counts would match.
Neither die favours big numbers. Look at how many pairs reach each total.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Count only matching pairs, then divide by all 36 pairs.
List the pairs for totals 10, 11 and 12, including reversed pairs.
There are three pairs for 10, two for 11 and one for 12; divide their combined count by the full grid count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Totals 10, 11 and 12 have 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes; 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: Six of 36: 3 + 2 + 1 pairs for 10, 11 and 12. The denominator stays every pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of pairs. A probability divides it by all the pairs.
That counts totals, not pairs. Totals are not equally likely, so count cells.

questions.prompt: So what is the probability that the total is below 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Subtract the probability of at least 10 from 1.
The events below 10 and at least 10 partition the full grid.
Subtract the six pairs at least 10 from the full count, then divide by the full count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The complement has 36 − 6 = 30 outcomes, so 30/36 = 5/6.

questions.onCorrect: Leave out the 6 pairs: 30 of 36. The complement is everything the event is not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of at least 10. This question asks about the pairs that are left.
That is a count of pairs. A probability divides by all the pairs.

questions.prompt: Two fair four-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List the pairs that sum to 5; the changed dice have four sides each.
The pairs (1,4) and (4,1) are distinct; include both middle pairs too.
Divide the four matching pairs by four first choices times four second choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four pairs make 5: (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1). There are 16 pairs, so 4/16 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: Four of 16 pairs: the grid is 4 × 4 now, and (1,4) and (4,1) count separately.

misconceptions.feedback: Check whether (1,4) and (4,1) are being counted as one pair. They are different outcomes.
36 belongs to six-sided dice. How many pairs do two four-sided dice make?

questions.prompt: When may you calculate probability by counting favourable outcomes over all outcomes?
hints: Counting gives each outcome the same weight.

acceptedIdeas: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The favourable-count divided by total-count shortcut requires equally likely outcomes. If their probabilities differ, add the probabilities of the favourable outcomes instead.

choices.label: Whenever the outcomes are equally likely
Whenever outcomes have numerical names
Only when the event is certain

questions.onCorrect: Counting favourable over all outcomes needs every outcome equally likely.

misconceptions.feedback: The names of the outcomes do not matter. What matters is whether each has the same chance.
Counting works for uncertain events too. The condition is about the outcomes' chances.

questions.prompt: You learn that the first roll is at most 2. How many ordered outcomes can still happen?
hints: Count only the two eligible rows.
The condition keeps two first-roll values; all second-roll values remain possible.
Multiply the two surviving rows by the six cells in each row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two first-roll values remain, each with six second rolls: 2 × 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. The clue removes whole rows; two rows of six pairs remain.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the grid before the clue. The clue crosses out whole rows.
That is one row. How many rows does the clue keep?

questions.prompt: Given a first roll of at most 2, what is the probability of a second roll of at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Restrict both counts to the surviving rows.
Each eligible row has three matching second-roll values.
Divide two rows times three matches by two rows times six eligible values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 6 matching pairs among 12 eligible pairs, so 6/12 = 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Half. Count inside the surviving rows: matches over the pairs the clue leaves.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36, the grid before the clue. Divide by what remains.
That counts matching pairs. A probability divides by the pairs still possible.

questions.prompt: Given a first roll of at most 2, what is the probability of a total of at least 7? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Count pairs in the two eligible rows that sum to at least 7.
In the row for first roll 1, only second roll 6 qualifies. In row 2, second rolls 5 and 6 qualify.
Divide the three matching cells by the count in two complete eligible rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matching pairs are (1,6), (2,5) and (2,6), so 3/12 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: A quarter. Look only in the two surviving rows, then divide by their 12 pairs.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts pairs in all six rows. The clue leaves only two.
That counts pairs. Divide by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: Now the first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is 7? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: A first roll of 1 fixes the row.
Only the first row remains; ask which second-roll value reaches the target.
One second-roll value qualifies among all six eligible second-roll values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (1,6) qualifies among the six possible pairs in the first row: 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: One of the six pairs in the surviving row. A tighter clue leaves a smaller list.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves one row of pairs.
One pair qualifies, but more than one is still possible.

questions.prompt: The first roll is known to be 1. What is the probability that the total is at least 5? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Which second rolls reach 5 when the first is 1?
Subtract the fixed first roll from the target sum to find the minimum second roll.
The qualifying second rolls are 4, 5 and 6; divide their count by all six possibilities.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second roll must be 4, 5 or 6. Three of six eligible outcomes qualify: 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Half. A second roll of 4, 5 or 6 reaches the total, out of six possible.

misconceptions.feedback: Other second rolls also reach the target. List which ones do.
Check the lowest second roll that reaches the target: a smaller one falls short.

questions.prompt: A clue rules out some outcomes. What goes on the bottom of the probability?
hints: The clue changes what is still possible.

acceptedIdeas: Only outcomes compatible with the clue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Conditioning restricts the sample space to outcomes compatible with the clue. Count favourable outcomes within that same restricted set.

choices.label: All outcomes before the clue
Only outcomes compatible with the clue
Only the favourable outcomes

questions.onCorrect: Count what is still possible. The denominator is the outcomes that fit the clue.

misconceptions.feedback: That denominator includes pairs the clue has ruled out, which cannot have happened.
Dividing favourable by favourable is always the same number. The denominator is everything still possible.

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice. What is the probability that both show at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Count the 3 by 3 square among all 36 pairs.
Each individual roll passes for three of its six possible values.
Multiply three-sixths by three-sixths, then simplify the resulting fraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each roll qualifies with probability 3/6 = 1/2; the joint probability is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: The 3 × 3 square is 9 of 36 cells, and 1/2 × 1/2 gives the same: independent chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die alone. Both dice have to pass, so the chance is smaller than that.
Adding the two chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: Now what is the probability that both dice show at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Each individual probability is 2/6.
The matching cells form a two-by-two square.
Divide the area of that square by the six-by-six full outcome count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 2 × 2 = 4 matching pairs, so 4/36 = 1/9.

questions.onCorrect: 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9. The four-cell square in the grid agrees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die. Both dice must pass.
That adds the two chances. Both must happen, so combine them another way.

questions.prompt: Why may you multiply the two chances?
hints: Independence concerns how a condition affects a probability.

acceptedIdeas: Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Events are independent when learning that one occurred does not change the other's probability, when the conditional probability is defined. Equivalently, their joint probability is the product.

choices.label: The events cannot happen together
Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
Both events have probability one half

questions.onCorrect: Learning that one event happened leaves the other's chance unchanged. That is why the chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: Events that cannot happen together are mutually exclusive, which is different.
Independence is about whether one result changes the other's chance, not how large the chances are.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that at least one of the two dice shows above 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Subtract the chance that both rolls are low from 1.
Its complement is both rolls at most 3.
Subtract nine matching low-low pairs from the full grid and divide by the full count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both rolls at most 3 has probability 1/4. Subtracting this from 1 gives 3/4.

questions.onCorrect: 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. “At least one” is the complement of “both low”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that both are low. The question asks about the pairs left over.
That is one die alone. Either die can be the high one.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed independently. What is the probability of two heads? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List ordered coin outcomes.
Keep HT and TH separate when listing the possible pairs.
Divide the one heads-heads outcome by the full ordered outcome count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only HH qualifies: 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. It matches the one HH in four equally likely results.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one coin. Both coins have to show heads.
HH, HT, TH and TT are four results, not three. Keep HT and TH separate.

questions.prompt: On a single die roll, the events 'roll 1' and 'roll 2' are which kind of pair?
hints: Can both events occur in one roll?

acceptedIdeas: Mutually exclusive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The events are mutually exclusive: one roll cannot be both 1 and 2. They are not independent, because knowing that 1 occurred makes the probability of 2 zero.

choices.label: Independent
Mutually exclusive
Identical

questions.onCorrect: One roll can't show both 1 and 2, so they are mutually exclusive. Knowing one happened rules out the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Independent events can happen together. Here both cannot happen on one roll.
These are two separate events. Ask whether both can occur on one roll.

questions.prompt: The last 5 becomes 25, so the values are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25. What happens to the mean and the median?
hints: Compare the total with the position of the middle value.

acceptedIdeas: The mean rises and the median stays 4
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replacing 5 with 25 increases the total and hence the mean. The sorted middle observation is still 4, so the median is unchanged.

choices.label: Both remain unchanged
The mean rises and the median stays 4
The median rises to 25

questions.onCorrect: The mean uses every value, so it rises. The median only needs the order, so it stays.

misconceptions.feedback: The total changes when one value changes, so the mean cannot stay put.
The median is a place in the sorted list, not the biggest value.

questions.prompt: Five friends have £2, £4, £4, £5 and £5. They pool the money and share it out equally. How much does each get?
hints: Add all five values, then divide by five.
There are five observations, including repeated values.
Divide the sum of all observations by their count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 20 across five observations, so the mean is 20/5 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: £4. Sharing the total equally is the mean: add everything, divide by how many.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole pot. Share it among the five friends.
That averages just two of the amounts. Pool the whole pot, then share it equally.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 2, 4, 4, 5 and 25?
hints: Find the middle position after sorting.
An odd-sized sorted dataset has a single middle position.
With five values, take the third value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The five sorted values have 4 in the third, middle position.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The 25 is the last value in order, so the middle is untouched.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 25 drags up. The median is the middle value.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 10, 2, 6 and 4?
hints: Average the middle pair, not the endpoints.
The even-sized sorted list has two middle positions.
Take the average of the second and third values, 4 and 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle pair is 4 and 6; its average is (4 + 6)/2 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Sort, then average the middle pair: (4 + 6) ÷ 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. The median averages only the middle pair.
Four values have two middle ones. Combine them.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Every observation contributes to the total.
There are five values, so the denominator is five.
Add 1 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 18 and divide the sum by five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 30, so the mean is 30/5 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The total is 30, shared over 5 values. The 18 pulls the mean up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle value, the median. The mean uses every value.
That is the total. Share it among the values.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the median is accurate?
hints: An even-sized dataset has two middle positions.

acceptedIdeas: For an even count it averages the two sorted middle values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sort the data before locating its centre. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle observations and need not itself be observed.

choices.label: It is always an observed value
It is always the largest value
For an even count it averages the two sorted middle values

questions.onCorrect: Sort first. With an even count, average the two middle values.

misconceptions.feedback: With an even count the middle falls between two values, so the median need not be one of them.
The largest value is the maximum. The median sits in the middle.

questions.prompt: The lists 4, 4, 4, 4 and 2, 2, 6, 6 are compared. What is the relationship?
hints: Work out each mean. Then look at where the points sit.

acceptedIdeas: The same mean, different spread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both lists average 4. The first has no deviation from it, while the second lies two below or above.

choices.label: The same mean, different spread
Different means, the same spread
Identical distributions

questions.onCorrect: Same mean of 4, different spread. A centre on its own cannot tell these lists apart.

misconceptions.feedback: Work out each mean first: do the lists really differ there?
Same average does not mean the points sit in the same places. Compare where they lie.

questions.prompt: What is the range of 2, 2, 6 and 6?
hints: Subtract the minimum from the maximum.
Repeated values do not change which endpoints are smallest and largest.
Subtract the smallest endpoint, 2, from the largest endpoint, 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The largest value is 6 and the smallest is 2; the range is 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The range is the largest minus the smallest, so the repeats make no difference.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two extremes. Compare them another way.
That is the largest value. Compare it with the smallest.

questions.prompt: What is the population standard deviation of 2, 2, 6 and 6?
hints: What is the mean? How far is each value from it?
Every value is the same distance from the mean. Square that distance.
The squares average to the variance. Take its square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All four squared distances from the mean 4 are 4. Variance is 16/4 = 4; its square root is 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Every value is 2 from the mean, so the squares average to 4 and the root is 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
That is the sum of the squared distances divided by two. Use the count of values.

questions.prompt: What is the population variance of 0, 0, 8 and 8?
hints: Square each distance from the mean of 4.
The mean is 4; compute the squared distance of each 0 and each 8.
Add those four squared distances and divide by the whole-population count of four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each squared distance from mean 4 is 16. Their average is 64/4 = 16.

questions.onCorrect: 16. Each value is 4 from the mean, and 4 × 4 is the squared distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the standard deviation. Variance is the average of the squared distances, before the root.
That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.

questions.prompt: What is the range of 3, 4, 4, 7 and 13?
hints: Only the two endpoints determine the range.
The interior values do not affect a range calculation.
Use only the maximum 13 and the minimum 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The maximum minus the minimum is 13 − 3 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. Only the largest and smallest count: 13 − 3. The middle values play no part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest value. The range compares it with the smallest.
That adds the extremes. The range is their difference.

questions.prompt: A list is a whole population, and a second list is a sample from a larger group. What differs in the variance?
hints: Is every member of the group in the list, or only some?

acceptedIdeas: A whole-population variance divides by its count; the usual sample estimate divides by one less
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: For the full population, divide the squared distances by their count. The usual estimate from a sample divides by one less, because the mean was itself estimated.

choices.label: Variance never uses a denominator
A whole-population variance divides by its count; the usual sample estimate divides by one less
Population variance divides only by the largest value

questions.onCorrect: A whole population divides by its count. A sample usually divides by one less.

misconceptions.feedback: Averaging means dividing by something. Ask what the squared distances are divided by.
The largest value has nothing to do with how many values there are.

questions.prompt: Here is a small population of shoppers. How many members does the whole population have?
hints: Count both groups, including unselected members.
The population includes the members without check marks too.
Add the morning group's size to the evening group's size.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The population contains six morning and six evening members: 6 + 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. The population includes everyone, checked or not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one group. The population has both groups.
That is part of a sample. The population is everyone, not only those checked.

questions.prompt: Six members are worth 2 and six are worth 8. What is the population mean?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Count each of the two group values six times.
Use (6 × 2 + 6 × 8) divided by the total number of members.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Total of 60 over 12 members, using everyone.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts once for every member.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A sample matches the population mean in one constructed example. What follows?
hints: One observed match cannot establish a general guarantee.

acceptedIdeas: It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Agreement in this constructed sample is evidence about this case only. It does not guarantee that another sample or another measured quantity will agree.

choices.label: It proves the method is unbiased in every population
It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere
It proves there is no sampling error

questions.onCorrect: One match shows agreement here. It does not guarantee agreement elsewhere.

misconceptions.feedback: One match in a made-up example cannot prove a method works in every population.
Sampling error is the chance gap between a sample and the population. One match does not remove it.

questions.prompt: A population has six members worth 4 and six worth 10. What is its mean?
hints: The two groups have equal size.
The group sizes are equal, so both contribute the same weight.
Use (6 × 4 + 6 × 10) divided by the combined group count.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The groups are equal in size, so the mean sits midway between the values.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A survey meant for a whole city reaches only weekday visitors to one gym. What is the main limitation?
hints: Compare the target population with the people the survey can reach.

acceptedIdeas: Other parts of the target population are systematically excluded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sampling frame omits people who do not visit that gym on weekdays. Increasing responses within that frame does not remove the systematic exclusion.

choices.label: Too many people were asked
Other parts of the target population are systematically excluded
Every city resident has the same inclusion chance

questions.onCorrect: The method leaves out other parts of the city, and more replies would not fix that.

misconceptions.feedback: Asking many people is not the problem. Ask who could never be asked.
Not every resident can be reached through one gym on weekdays.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a probability sample?
hints: Known inclusion probabilities do not have to be equal.

acceptedIdeas: Selection by chance with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A probability sample uses chance selection with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities. Those probabilities can differ between units; equal probabilities are a special case.

choices.label: Any sample collected quickly
Selection by chance with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities
Only volunteers who already agree

questions.onCorrect: Chance selection with known, non-zero chances of inclusion makes a probability sample.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed is not the test. A probability sample is chosen by chance.
Volunteers choose themselves. A probability sample uses chance with known probabilities.

questions.prompt: Why sort the values before picking the middle one?
hints: Is the middle of the list as written the middle in size?

acceptedIdeas: The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The median is the middle in size order. The order the values were written down tells you nothing about that.

choices.label: The middle means the middle in size, not in the order written
Sorting changes the median
The mean needs the values in order

questions.onCorrect: The median is the middle in size order, so the list must be in that order first.

misconceptions.feedback: Sorting only puts the values in order. It doesn't change them.
The mean doesn't depend on order. It is only the median that does.

questions.prompt: What is the sum of the two middle values, 4 and 6? Write the number.
hints: Which two values are the middle pair of four?
Add the second value and the third.
Add the two middle values only.
questions.onCorrect: 10. The median of an even list starts from the middle pair's total.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds all four values. Only the middle pair goes in.

questions.prompt: Five houses sell for these prices, in thousands of pounds: 180, 190, 200, 210 and 720. What is the median price, in thousands?
hints: Are the prices in order? Which is in the middle?
Five values: the middle is the third.
The third price in order is the one you want.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sorted already; the third of five is 200.

questions.onCorrect: 200. The 720 sits at the end of the list and cannot move the middle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 720 drags up. The median is the middle price.
That is the largest price. The median is the middle one in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 3, 3, 5 and 18?
hints: Are the values in order?
Five values: which position is the middle?
Take the third value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third of five sorted values is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Compare it with the mean of 6: the 18 drags the mean and leaves the median.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which uses every value. The median is the middle one.
That is the largest value. The median is the middle in size order.

questions.prompt: What is the median of 1, 2 and 9?
hints: Is the list in order?
Three values: which position is the middle?
Take the middle value of the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sorted middle of three values is 2.

questions.onCorrect: The middle of the sorted list. The 9 does not move it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean, which the 9 drags up. The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A coin is flipped twice. HT means heads, then tails. How many different results can you get, counting HT and TH as different?
hints: Write them out: start with the ones that begin with heads.
Two begin with H. How many begin with T?
List HH, HT, then the two that begin with T.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HH, HT, TH and TT: 4 results.

questions.onCorrect: 4: HH, HT, TH, TT. Listing every result is where probability starts.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts how many heads you might see: none, one or two. HT and TH are different results, so list the order too.
Each flip has two sides, but the flips go together. List what the pair of flips can show.

questions.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is not 12? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: How many of the 36 pairs make a total of 12?
Only one pair makes 12. How many pairs are left over?
Count the pairs that are not 12, then divide by all the pairs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only (6,6) makes 12, so 36 − 1 = 35 pairs do not: 35/36.

questions.onCorrect: 35/36. Count what the event leaves out, then divide by every pair: the complement.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the probability of a total of 12. The question asks about every other pair.
That treats the eleven possible totals as equally likely. Count pairs instead: some totals have more than one.

questions.prompt: How many ordered pairs make a total of 8?
hints: Start with a first roll of 2. What second roll makes 8?
Work along the first rolls. Does a first roll of 1 have a partner?
The pairs run (2,6) to (6,2). Count them.
questions.onCorrect: 5 pairs. Each first roll from 2 to 6 has exactly one partner.

misconceptions.feedback: A first roll of 1 would need a second roll of 7. Check which first rolls have a partner.
Count (4,4) too, and keep both (2,6) and (6,2).

questions.prompt: What is the probability that the total is 8? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Use the count you just made.
Divide the pairs that make 8 by all the pairs.
Your count goes on top; the bottom is every ordered pair.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 pairs out of 36: 5/36.

questions.onCorrect: 5/36. Pairs that make 8, over every equally likely pair.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 6 ÷ 36. Use the number of pairs that make 8, not 6.
That treats the eleven possible totals as equally likely. Divide by the number of pairs.

questions.prompt: Two coins are flipped. What is the probability of exactly one head? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List all four results.
Which of the four results have exactly one head?
Put the number of those results over the number of all results.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: HT and TH are 2 of the 4 results: 2/4.

questions.onCorrect: Exactly one head holds two of the four outcomes. Count the event, divide by all.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts one outcome. The event holds more than one.
TT is a result too. Count every equally likely result, not just the ones with heads.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin and roll a die. One result is heads with a 3. How many different results are there?
hints: List the results that start with heads. How many are there?
Each coin result pairs with every die result.
Heads pairs with six die results. Tails does too.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 coin results × 6 die results = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12: every coin result pairs with every die result. Keep that grid in mind.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sides: 2 + 6. Each coin result pairs with every die result, so think of a grid.
That is only the heads results. Tails pairs with the die results as well.

questions.prompt: One fair die is rolled. What is the probability that it shows at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Which values are at most 2?
Two of the six values qualify.
Put the number of qualifying values over the number of values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two of six values: 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: 1/3. Two of the six equally likely values qualify.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts values. A probability divides by the six possible values.
Count 1 and 2 both; two values qualify.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and a number above 4? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Find each chance alone: tails, then a number above 4.
Tails is one of two results. Which die numbers are above 4?
The two chances are independent, so combine them with the rule from the worked example.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tails is 1/2. A 5 or 6 is 2/6 = 1/3. Together: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: 1/6. The coin and die are independent, so multiply 1/2 by 1/3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of not getting both. Multiply the two separate chances.
Adding the chances is for exclusive events. Here both must happen: multiply them.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of three heads? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: One flip shows heads with probability 1/2. Does the first flip change the second?
The flips are independent. How many chances do you multiply?
Multiply the chance for each flip together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each flip is 1/2 and the flips are independent: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

questions.onCorrect: 1/8. Independent flips multiply: each extra heads halves the chance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one flip. All three have to be heads, which makes the chance smaller.
That is two flips. There is a third to include.
Adding the chances gives more than 1, which can't be a probability. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and an even number? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Find the chance of tails alone, then of an even number alone.
Even numbers on a die are 2, 4 and 6. What fraction is that?
The two are independent, so combine the two chances as the lesson says.
questions.onCorrect: Independent chances multiply: 1/2 × 1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two chances. Both must happen.
Adding the chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: One die is rolled. Are “shows 1” and “shows an even number” mutually exclusive?
hints: Is the number 1 odd or even?

acceptedIdeas: Yes: one roll cannot be both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1 is odd, so a roll cannot show 1 and an even number together.

choices.label: Yes: one roll cannot be both
No: both can happen on one roll

questions.onCorrect: Yes. One roll cannot be both, so they are mutually exclusive.

misconceptions.feedback: The first number is odd. Ask whether a roll can be odd and even at once.

questions.prompt: Bus A is exactly 10 minutes late on each of four days. Bus B is late by 0, 0, 20 and 20 minutes. Both average 10 minutes. What is the gap between Bus B's best day and its worst day, in minutes?
hints: Which day was Bus B's best, the least late?
Its worst day is the most late. How many minutes is that?
Take the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 − 0 = 20 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: 20 minutes. Bus A has no gap at all, though both buses average the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Bus B's average. The question compares its two extreme days.
That is the total lateness over four days. Compare only the best and worst days.

questions.prompt: Why square each distance from the mean?
hints: Add the distances 1 − 3, 1 − 3, 1 − 3 and 9 − 3. What do you notice?

acceptedIdeas: Distances below the mean would cancel distances above it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Distances below the mean are negative and above are positive, so they cancel. Squares are never negative.

choices.label: Distances below the mean would cancel distances above it
Squaring makes every number smaller
The mean is always a square

questions.onCorrect: Distances below the mean cancel distances above. Squares are never negative, so they all count.

misconceptions.feedback: Squaring a number above 1 makes it bigger. Think about the signs of the distances.
The mean can be any number. Think about what happens to negative distances.

questions.prompt: Each squared distance is 4. What is the total of the four squared distances?
hints: Four equal numbers are added.
Four lots of the same number: use multiplication.
Multiply the squared distance by how many values there are.
questions.onCorrect: 16. Add the squared distances; the next move is to average them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one squared distance. Add all four.

questions.prompt: Average the four squared distances. What is the population variance?
hints: Divide the total by how many values there are.
Four values, so divide by four.
Take the total of the squares and share it over the four values.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Variance is the average squared distance from the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.
Dividing by one less is for samples. This list is the whole population.

questions.prompt: Bus B is late 0, 0, 20 and 20 minutes, a whole population. What is its population standard deviation, in minutes?
hints: Find the mean first. How far is each day from it?
Square that distance, then average the squares.
The average of the squares is the variance. Take its square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each day is 10 from the mean, squares 100, variance 100, standard deviation 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10 minutes. Bus A has none at all: that is the difference the mean hides.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. Take its square root to return to minutes.
That is the range. Use every day's distance from the mean instead.

questions.prompt: What is the population standard deviation of 3, 3, 9 and 9?
hints: Find the mean first.
Every value is the same distance from the mean. Square that distance.
The squares average to the variance. Its square root is the standard deviation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 6, every value is 3 away, variance 9, standard deviation 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The mean is 6 and every value is 3 away, so the root of the average square is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
That is the mean. Spread is about distance from it.

questions.prompt: The squared distances from the mean of a whole population are 2, 4 and 6. What is the variance?
hints: The variance is the average of the squared distances.
Add the squared distances, then divide by how many there are.
Divide the total of the squares by three.
questions.onCorrect: The variance is the average squared distance from the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the squares. Divide by how many values there are.
That divides by two. Use the count of values.

questions.prompt: A shop has 12 customers. Six are morning shoppers who each spend £2. Six are evening shoppers who each spend £8. You ask only the morning shoppers. What average spend do you find?
hints: Who does your survey reach?
Every morning shopper spends the same amount.
The average of identical amounts is that amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All six morning shoppers spend £2, so the average is £2.

questions.onCorrect: £2. The survey was honest and still missed half the customers.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the average of every customer. Your survey only reaches the morning shoppers.
That is the evening shoppers. They were not asked.

questions.prompt: A town has 5,000 homes and a survey asks 200 of them. How many homes are in the sample?
hints: Which homes were actually asked?
Is the sample the whole town or part of it?
Count the homes that were asked.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sample is the 200 homes that were asked.

questions.onCorrect: 200. The sample is the part you measure; the 5,000 homes are the population.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the population, everyone you want to learn about. The sample is the part you measure.

questions.prompt: Why count both groups when finding the population mean?
hints: Who does the population include?

acceptedIdeas: The population is everyone you want to learn about
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population is the whole target set, so every member of both groups belongs in it.

choices.label: The population is everyone you want to learn about
The larger group always counts more
Samples must have equal groups

questions.onCorrect: The population is everyone you want to learn about, so both groups count.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the groups are the same size. The population is defined by who you want to learn about.
This is about the population, not the sample. A sample need not be balanced.

questions.prompt: Six members are worth 2 and six are worth 8. What is the total of all twelve values?
hints: Six members are worth the first amount each.
Find six lots of each value, then add.
Add six times the first value to six times the second.
questions.onCorrect: 60. Count each group value once per member.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted once for every member.

questions.prompt: A balanced sample takes three members from each group, worth 2 and 8. What is the sample mean?
hints: Add the six sampled values.
Three lots of the first value plus three lots of the second.
Divide the total by the six members sampled.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Half from each group balances out to the middle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted three times.
That is the total. Divide by the six members sampled.

questions.prompt: A population has four members worth 3 and four worth 9. What is its mean?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Four lots of each value, added.
Divide the total by the number of members.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Total over members, using the whole population.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is one group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: Two coins are flipped. You are told that at least one landed heads. How many of the four results HH, HT, TH and TT could still have happened?
hints: Cross out any result with no heads in it.
Which of the four has no heads at all?
Take TT out of the list and count what is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: TT has no heads, so HH, HT and TH remain: 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The clue crossed out TT and left a shorter list. That list is where the next probability lives.

misconceptions.feedback: TT has no heads, so it cannot match the clue. Cross it out.
Check HH as well as the mixed results: which of the four fit the clue?

questions.prompt: Why divide by 12 and not by 36?
hints: Which pairs can still have happened once you know the first roll?

acceptedIdeas: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Once the first roll is known to be at most 2, only the pairs in those two rows are possible.

choices.label: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only 12 can have happened
Twelve is always the denominator
Dividing by 36 gives a smaller number, which is safer

questions.onCorrect: The clue rules out the other pairs, so only the pairs in the surviving rows can have happened.

misconceptions.feedback: The denominator is whatever the clue leaves possible, and that changes with the clue.
A probability is not chosen to be small. It has to count what is actually possible.

questions.prompt: How many of the 12 remaining pairs have a second roll of at most 3?
hints: Look at one surviving row. How many second rolls are at most 3?
Each row has the same count. How many rows survive?
Multiply the matches in one row by the number of rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 matching second rolls in each of 2 rows: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Count favourable pairs inside the surviving rows only.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one row. Two rows survive.
That is every remaining pair. Count only those with a second roll of at most 3.

questions.prompt: The first roll is at least 5. What is the probability that the total is at least 10? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Which first rolls does the clue allow? How many pairs is that?
List the pairs inside those rows that total 10 or more.
Count them and divide by the pairs the clue allows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rows 5 and 6 give 12 pairs. Totals of at least 10 come from (5,5), (5,6), (6,4), (6,5) and (6,6): 5 of 12.

questions.onCorrect: 5/12. Restrict to the two rows the clue allows, then count inside them.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 36. The clue leaves only two rows.
That is the number of matching pairs. Divide by the pairs the clue leaves.

questions.prompt: A die is rolled and you are told the result is even. How many results can still have happened?
hints: Which results are even?
List the even numbers on a die.
Count the even numbers on the die.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2, 4 and 6: 3 results.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The clue left a shorter list of results.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the list before the clue. The clue rules some out.
More than one even result is possible.

flashcards.front: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled independently. What is the probability of a total of 3?
flashcards.back: The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) give 3, so the probability is 2/36 = 1/18.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) give 3, so the probability is 2/36 = 1/18.

flashcards.front: What is the name for the event consisting of all outcomes outside event A?
flashcards.back: The complement of A consists of the outcomes where A does not occur.

acceptedIdeas: complement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The complement of A consists of the outcomes where A does not occur.

flashcards.front: Two fair dice are rolled independently. Given a first roll of 1, what is the probability of a sum of 4?
flashcards.back: Only a second roll of 3 gives 4. One of the six eligible outcomes qualifies: 1/6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only a second roll of 3 gives 4. One of the six eligible outcomes qualifies: 1/6.

flashcards.front: What kind of probability uses a sample space restricted by a known event?
flashcards.back: Conditional probability restricts the possible outcomes to those compatible with the given event.

acceptedIdeas: conditional
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Conditional probability restricts the possible outcomes to those compatible with the given event.

flashcards.front: Two fair six-sided rolls are independent. What is the probability that both equal 6?
flashcards.back: Each roll has probability 1/6, so both have probability 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each roll has probability 1/6, so both have probability 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

flashcards.front: What term describes two events that cannot both happen in the same trial?
flashcards.back: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together; that is different from independence.

acceptedIdeas: mutually exclusive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together; that is different from independence.

courseChecks.title: Find your starting point
courseChecks.description: Six problems about chance, data and sampling. Use the stated assumptions and see which lessons will help.

question.prompt: Two fair spinners are independent. What is the probability that their numbers sum to 5? Give a fraction or decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 3 × 4 = 12 equally likely ordered pairs. (1,4), (2,3) and (3,2) sum to 5, giving 3/12 = 1/4.

question.prompt: A person is selected uniformly from the evening group. What is the probability they passed?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The condition restricts the denominator to the 20 evening members. Nine passed, so the probability is 9/20.

question.prompt: Assume the two sensors work independently. What is the probability that both work?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Independence permits multiplying the two probabilities: 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48.

question.prompt: What is the median of these five observations?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sorting gives 4, 5, 7, 8, 11. The middle observation is 7.

question.prompt: These four values are the entire population. What is their population variance?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 6. Each squared deviation is 9, so their sum 36 divided by the population size 4 gives variance 9.

question.prompt: Roll two independent fair six-sided dice. What is the probability of a total of 9 or 10?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four ordered pairs total 9 and three total 10. These cases do not overlap, giving 7 favourable pairs out of 36.

question.prompt: The table describes every member of a small population. What is the population mean value?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The total is 3 × 2 + 9 × 6 = 60 across 12 members. The mean is 60/12 = 5; averaging the two group values without their sizes would give the wrong weight.

question.prompt: Choose one tile uniformly from all tiles, then learn that it is triangular. What is the probability it is red?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are four triangular tiles and three are red. The square tiles are outside the conditioned sample space.

question.prompt: Use all four values as the entire population. What is the population variance?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 4. Squared deviations are 4, 0, 0 and 4. Their sum 8 divided by all four population members gives variance 2.

question.prompt: One of the 15 codes is chosen uniformly. What is the probability its letter is B or its number is 5?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The five B codes and the three codes ending in 5 overlap at B5. Count it once: 5 + 3 - 1 = 7 favourable codes out of 15.

question.prompt: These are the complete four readings for a batch. What is their population standard deviation?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is 10 and every reading is 3 away. Population variance is 9, whose square root is 3.

statements.label: B

question.prompt: Every household has a known, nonzero selection probability, but some probabilities are larger. Which statement is justified?

acceptedIdeas: It is a probability sample, but unequal chances can require weighting for population estimates.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A probability sample requires known, nonzero chances, not identical ones. Unequal probabilities matter when estimating population quantities; no one realised sample is guaranteed to match everything.

choices.label: This cannot be a probability sample because the chances differ.
It is a probability sample, but unequal chances can require weighting for population estimates.
Every resulting sample must match every population characteristic exactly.

question.prompt: In this model, rainy days are independent, each with probability 1/4. What is the probability of rain on at least one of two days?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No rain on either day has probability (3/4) × (3/4) = 9/16. Its complement is 1 - 9/16 = 7/16. Independence is a stated model assumption, not a claim about real weather.

question.prompt: Six waiting times are shown. What is their median, in minutes?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ordered middle values are 5 and 6. Their average is 5.5 minutes; the longest wait does not change which pair is central.

question.prompt: Select a tested item uniformly, then learn that it failed. What is the probability it came from line B?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three failed items in total, one from line B. Conditioning on failure gives 1/3; the total number tested is no longer the denominator.
